objection: If Jesus is God, why did he pray to God?
answer: This is a fair challenge, and I don't want to minimize the rawness of Gethsemane. But notice what orthodoxy has always said: Christ is one person with two natures, and the anguish in the garden belongs to his genuine humanity, not a diminishment of his deity. John 17 shows Jesus praying to the Father while the same Gospel opens by declaring the Word was God and closes with Thomas confessing him "my Lord and my God" (John 20:28) — the Evangelist saw no contradiction between prayer and deity, because the prayer flows from the Son's human nature and the personal relation of Son to Father, not from an inferior divine essence. The Son who is co-equal with the Father nonetheless has a real human will, a real body capable of dread, a real soul capable of sorrow unto death — that is what it means for the Word to become flesh. Petition in the garden reveals the same self-giving obedience seen throughout his life: as Son he defers to the Father not because he is less God, but because that is the eternal shape of their relation, now lived out under the weight of an actual human nature bearing actual suffering. Notably, this is not the whole picture the earliest church left us: those same early Christians who preserved the memory of Gethsemane also called upon Jesus in prayer as Lord — Stephen dying with "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59), and the Aramaic Maranatha, "our Lord, come," embedded already in 1 Corinthians 16:22. A community that remembered him pleading in anguish is the very same community that addressed him as the one to be pled to. That combination — Jesus praying as man, and Jesus being prayed to as God — is not incoherent; it is precisely the mystery the incarnation predicts.

Here's the objection in character:

Look, if Jesus is truly God—fully divine, coequal with the Father—we have a real problem with the prayer accounts. In Gethsemane, Mark has him begging "Abba, Father, let this cup pass from me" (14:36); in Luke, he's in such anguish an angel has to strengthen him. A being who is omniscient and omnipotent doesn't plead with someone else to change outcomes; that's the posture of a creature dependent on a greater power. The earliest layer shows a human under duress appealing to God—which is exactly what you'd expect if the memory was of a righteous man, later deified by his followers. How do you square genuine, desperate petitionary prayer with the claim that he was the ultimate reality himself?
